newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Experts urge Ukraine to aid Chernobyl victims more.
newsitem.headline: Experts urge Ukraine to aid Chernobyl victims more.

text.p: Ukrainian health experts, painting a picture of an increasingly sick population on the eve of the 11th anniversary of the Chernobyl nuclear accident, urged the government on Wednesday to increase aid to victims.
"Only 35 to 40 percent of what is needed is being covered..," Olha Boboleva, chief of the Health Ministry's Chernobyl department, told a news conference.
"But cases of cancer and thyroid problems are increasing," she said.

Cash-strapped Ukraine, which gained independence in 1991, has been left to foot a bill estimated at 12 percent of its annual budget to provide health care and benefits to victims of the Soviet-era disaster on April 26, 1986.
Boboleva said a high number of liquidators -- the scores of people sent in to clean up immediately after the disaster -- were sick, as were their children.
She partly blamed shortages of pure, unradiated food in the contaminated zones surrounding Chernobyl, where people still live, for the rise in illness.
"There is a need to increase health care," she said.

Ukrainian estimates show about two million of its 52 million people live in contaminated areas around Chernobyl, including 479 people who have returned voluntarily to live in the 30-km (19-mile) exclusion zone around the nuclear site.

A delegation from the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations met this week to hammer out an agreement to close Chernobyl, which President Leonid Kuchma has promised to shut by 2000 for $3.1 billion in Western credits.
Volodymyr Yatsenko, chief of parliament's Chernobyl committee, said two of nine proposed new tax laws would halve the money granted to victims every year.
"Ukraine is in an economic crisis and during the last five years funding to Chernobyl projects has been cut tenfold," he said, adding that some families were still awaiting relocation to safer areas.

Officials said funding was being cut to Chernobyl programmes not only because of the poor state of the economy but also to stop businesses illegally taking advantage of tax breaks granted to foreign charities bringing aid to victims.

The Emergencies Ministry announced this week a Chernobyl strategy to keep moving people out of contaminated zones, providing proper health care to victims, setting up facilities to decontaminate food and improving the area's ecological state.
The G7 countries are expected to decide on funding arrangements for Chernobyl's closure at a summit in June in the U.S. city of Denver.
Part of the deal is for the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) to build two new reactors at Khmelnytsky and Rivne in western Ukraine to replace the ruined Chernobyl reactor.
Ukrainian officials say more than 4,000 deaths can be attributed to the blast, which also spewed radiation over neighbouring Belarus and Russia.
